Credentials and networks

Source: vignettes/credentials-and-networks.Rmd
credentials-and-networks.Rmd

The Locator API only answers requests that carry a client ID and a client token, and only from some networks. This article covers how to get the credentials, where to keep them, how to keep the token safe, and what to do when the network is the problem.

Getting credentials

HIV.gov issues a client ID and a client token on request. The Locator page on HIV.gov says how to ask; in November 2026 it pointed to contact@hiv.gov. Keep the email they send: it is your only record of the token.

The ID identifies you, and the token works like a password. The package sends both with every request, in HTTP headers.

Where the package looks

Each function that calls the API (cdc_providers(), cdc_address_place() and cdc_address_point()) finds credentials in this order:

  1. The client_id and client_token arguments, if you pass them.
  2. The environment variables CDC_LOCATOR_CLIENT_ID and CDC_LOCATOR_CLIENT_TOKEN.

If neither is set, it stops with “CDC Locator API credentials not found” and sends nothing.

Option 1: your .Renviron file (recommended)

R reads .Renviron each time it starts, so credentials stored there are always available and never appear in your code.

The quickest way to save them there is to let the package do it. It asks first, names the file, and writes only after you answer yes:

cdc_locator_set_credentials(
  client_id = rstudioapi::askForPassword("Locator client ID"),
  client_token = rstudioapi::askForPassword("Locator client token"),
  install = TRUE
)

This works only in an interactive session, because it has to ask. It saves to .Renviron in your home folder, or to the file R_ENVIRON_USER names if you’ve set that. It replaces any CDC_LOCATOR_* lines already there and keeps everything else. Before writing anything secret, it makes the file readable only by you, and if it can’t, it saves nothing. On Windows, the permissions of your home folder protect it. It also sets the credentials for the current session, so you don’t need to restart R. If the current folder has its own .Renviron, it warns you, for the reason explained under “Which .Renviron R reads” below.

install = TRUE only saves plain values: letters, digits and . _ ~ + / = : -. If your ID or token has other characters, add it yourself.

To edit the file yourself instead, open it with:

usethis::edit_r_environ()

Add two lines, with your own values and no quotes:

CDC_LOCATOR_CLIENT_ID=your-client-id
CDC_LOCATOR_CLIENT_TOKEN=your-client-token

Save the file, make sure it ends with a blank line, and restart R. Then check, without printing the values:

nzchar(Sys.getenv(c("CDC_LOCATOR_CLIENT_ID", "CDC_LOCATOR_CLIENT_TOKEN")))

Both should be TRUE.

Which .Renviron R reads

R reads one user .Renviron file when it starts, not several:

  1. the file named by the R_ENVIRON_USER environment variable, if it’s set;
  2. otherwise, a .Renviron in the folder R starts in, which in RStudio is the project’s folder;
  3. otherwise, the .Renviron in your home folder.

So if a project has its own .Renviron, R uses that file instead of the one in your home folder, and credentials stored only in the home file are missing in that project. Either add the two lines to the project’s file too, or keep them only in the home file and don’t give the project its own.

usethis::edit_r_environ() opens the home file, and usethis::edit_r_environ(scope = "project") opens the project’s. If you use a project file, add .Renviron to the project’s .gitignore so it is never committed. To work out which file R would have read, check:

Sys.getenv("R_ENVIRON_USER")   # if set, R read this file
file.exists(".Renviron")       # is there a .Renviron in the current folder?

If R_ENVIRON_USER is empty and the current folder is still the one R started in (in RStudio, the project’s folder), a TRUE from file.exists() means R read that local file rather than the one in your home folder.

Option 2: for one session

cdc_locator_set_credentials() without install = TRUE sets both environment variables until R restarts. It never prints them and writes no file:

cdc_locator_set_credentials(
  client_id = "your-client-id",
  client_token = "your-client-token"
)

Typing the token into a script puts it wherever the script goes. To avoid that, read it at run time instead, for example with rstudioapi::askForPassword() or the keyring package:

cdc_locator_set_credentials(
  client_id = rstudioapi::askForPassword("Locator client ID"),
  client_token = rstudioapi::askForPassword("Locator client token")
)

Option 3: pass them to each call

Every function that calls the API takes client_id and client_token arguments. These override the environment variables for that call only. This is mainly useful when one script uses two sets of credentials.

Keeping the token safe

  • Keep it out of code. Don’t type it into scripts, R Markdown files or Quarto documents you might share.
  • Keep it out of Git. Never commit .Renviron. If a token is committed by mistake, removing it in a later commit doesn’t remove it from the history: ask HIV.gov for a new one.
  • Use secret storage for automation. On GitHub Actions, store the two values as repository secrets and pass them to the job as environment variables.

The package helps too: it marks both headers as secret, so printing a request or turning on verbose output shows <REDACTED>, and it removes both values from any error text the API sends back before showing it.

Which networks the API accepts

In November 2026, the API refused some networks with HTTP 403 Forbidden, even with valid credentials:

  • Outside the US: requests from a Canadian server got a “blocked from your country” page.
  • Some cloud servers in the US: GitHub Actions runners hosted on Microsoft Azure were refused, while runners on Amazon Web Services and a home internet connection worked with the same credentials.

These were observations on particular days, not rules HIV.gov has published, and they may change. In practice:

  • A home or office connection in the US has worked.
  • A VPN may route you through a server the API refuses. If you get a 403 on a VPN, try without it.
  • A cloud service (Posit Cloud, a hosted RStudio Server, Google Colab, a cloud virtual machine, GitHub Actions) may be refused. Whether it is depends on which provider and region it runs on.

Telling a network refusal from a key problem

Both give HTTP 403, and the package’s error lists both causes. To tell them apart:

  1. Read the API’s message in the error. A refused key has come back with a short message such as “User is not authorized to access this resource”. The country block came back as a web page, which the package doesn’t show, so that error has no “The API said” line. What the cloud-server refusals said wasn’t recorded, so a message alone may not settle it.
  2. Try a different network. If the same credentials work from a home connection, the network was the problem.
  3. Check the credentials themselves: no extra spaces or quotes in .Renviron, and R restarted after editing it.

If the credentials fail from a network that has worked before, contact HIV.gov: the token may have expired or been revoked.
